title: Introduction to Functions
learningObjective: Determine if a relation, equation, or graph defines a function using the definition as well as the vertical line test.

faqs.question: What is a relation?
faqs.answer: A relation is any set of ordered pairs (x, y): a pairing of inputs with outputs. Any collection of ordered pairs (x, y) is a relation. Think of it as a rule—or even just a list—that pairs inputs with outputs. Every function is a relation, but not every relation is a function. Relations are the bigger family; functions are a special subset with stricter rules.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a relation and a function?
faqs.answer: A relation is any set of ordered pairs—there are no restrictions. A function is a relation with one extra rule: every input (x-value) must produce exactly one output (y-value). Think of it like a vending machine. If you press B3, you expect one specific item to drop. If pressing B3 sometimes gave you chips and sometimes gave you a candy bar, you wouldn't trust the machine. Functions are trustworthy—one input, one output, every time.

faqs.question: What is the domain? What is the range?
faqs.answer: Extension: domain and range go beyond the FN1 CheckIt exercise (they come back in FN3). The domain is the set of all possible input values (x-values) for a relation or function. The range is the set of all possible output values (y-values). A helpful way to remember: the domain is what you're allowed to put in, and the range is what you get out. When listing domain and range, we write each value only once—no repeats—and typically list them in order from least to greatest.

faqs.question: Why does a function need exactly one output for each input?
faqs.answer: Because the whole point of a function is predictability. In math, science, and everyday life, we need to trust that the same input always gives us the same result. If you plug x = 3 into a function, you need to get one specific answer—not two or three possibilities. That's what makes functions useful for modeling the real world: they let us predict the output from the input.

faqs.question: Can two different inputs have the same output and still be a function?
faqs.answer: Yes! This is one of the most common misconceptions. A function only requires that each input has one output. There's no rule against multiple inputs sharing the same output. For example, think of item → price at a snack bar: a granola bar and a bottle of water can both cost $1.50. Each item still has exactly one price, so it is a function: different inputs, same output. The problem only arises when one input tries to map to multiple outputs.

faqs.question: What is a mapping diagram and why do we use it?
faqs.answer: A mapping diagram (also called an arrow diagram) shows how inputs connect to outputs. The inputs go in one oval and the outputs in another, with an arrow from each input to its output. It makes the structure visible: you can see at a glance whether any input has two arrows leaving it, which would mean it is not a function. Two arrows landing on the same output is fine, and so is an output with no arrow at all. CheckIt's mapping diagrams often have outputs like that.

faqs.question: Why is it okay for y-values to repeat but not x-values?
faqs.answer: The function rule is about inputs, not outputs. The rule says: each input gets exactly one output. It says nothing about outputs being unique. Think about a class roster—multiple students (inputs) can share the same birthday (output), and that's no problem. But one student can't have two different birthdays. That's the same logic: repeated y-values are fine, repeated x-values with different y-values are not.

faqs.question: How do I use the vertical line test?
faqs.answer: Imagine sliding a vertical line across the graph from left to right. At every position, ask: does this vertical line touch the graph in more than one place? If it ever hits two or more points, then one x-value has multiple y-values—and the relation is NOT a function. If every vertical line touches the graph at most once (once, or not at all), it IS a function. A vertical line that misses the graph completely is fine: that x-value just isn't an input. The key insight: vertical lines represent a single x-value, so if the line hits the graph twice, that x-value has two outputs.

faqs.question: How do I know if an equation is a function without graphing it?
faqs.answer: Solve for y, or test whether some x gives two different y-values. Plugging in a few x-values can show that an equation is NOT a function (one x with two y's is enough), but a few good tests can't prove it IS one; solving for y can. In the FN1 CheckIt equations, y appears in a single term, so the power on y decides it: an odd power (y^3, y^5, y^7) is undone by an odd root, which gives exactly one y, so it is a function. An even power (y^2, y^4, y^6) needs ±, so some x gives two y's, and it is not a function. For example, x = y^2 is not a function, because x = 4 gives y = 2 or y = −2. But y = x^2 IS a function: any x gives exactly one y. Careful with signs: in 2y^4 + 3x^5 = 0, positive x gives no y at all, so test a negative x.

faqs.question: Why does a y² often make an equation not a function?
faqs.answer: When you solve for a squared variable, you have to consider both the positive and negative square root. For example, if x = y², and you plug in x = 9, then y² = 9, which means y = 3 or y = −3. That's two outputs for one input—which violates the function rule. This is why equations like x = y² and x² + y² = 25 (a circle) are not functions. Whenever solving for y needs a ± step and the other side can be positive, one input gets two outputs.

faqs.question: What makes a value 'undefined'?
faqs.answer: Extension: undefined values and domain go beyond the FN1 CheckIt exercise. So far, two situations make an expression undefined: dividing by zero, and taking the square root of a negative number. Division by zero is undefined because a/0 would have to be a number that gives a when multiplied by 0: if a isn't 0, no number works, and if a is 0, every number works, so there is no single answer. Square roots of negative numbers are undefined (in real numbers) because no real number times itself gives a negative result. When finding domain, you're looking for x-values that avoid both of these situations.

faqs.question: How do I find the domain of a function with a square root?
faqs.answer: Extension: domain and range go beyond the FN1 CheckIt exercise (they come back in FN3). Set the expression inside the square root (or any even root) greater than or equal to zero, then solve. For example, for f(x) = √(x − 2), set x − 2 ≥ 0, which gives x ≥ 2. In interval notation: [2, ∞). The bracket on 2 means 2 is included (since √0 = 0 is defined). Remember: the inside of a square root cannot be negative, but it can be zero.

faqs.question: How do I find the domain of a function with a fraction?
faqs.answer: Extension: domain and range go beyond the FN1 CheckIt exercise (they come back in FN3). Set the denominator equal to zero and solve—those are the values you must exclude. For example, for f(x) = 3/(x − 5), set x − 5 = 0, so x = 5 is excluded. The domain is all real numbers except 5, written as (−∞, 5) ∪ (5, ∞). If the function also has a square root, handle both restrictions: the expression under the root can't be negative, and the denominator can't be zero. When the square root is itself in the denominator, the two rules combine: the expression under it must be strictly positive.

faqs.question: How do I write domain in interval notation?
faqs.answer: Extension: domain and range go beyond the FN1 CheckIt exercise (they come back in FN3). Interval notation uses parentheses ( ) for values that are NOT included and brackets [ ] for values that ARE included. Infinity always gets a parenthesis because you can never reach it. Use ∪ (union) to join separate intervals. Examples: all real numbers = (−∞, ∞). All numbers greater than or equal to 2 = [2, ∞). All numbers except 5 = (−∞, 5) ∪ (5, ∞). Think of parentheses as 'get close but don't touch' and brackets as 'this value is included.'

faqs.question: Why do functions matter—what's the point?
faqs.answer: Functions are the language of change. Nearly everything you'll study in this course—and in calculus—is built on functions. When scientists model population growth, when engineers design a bridge, when economists predict market trends, they're all using functions. The reason we spend time learning to identify and analyze functions now is that every major concept in precalculus (transformations, trigonometry, exponential growth, limits) depends on understanding how inputs relate to outputs.

faqs.question: How will I use functions later in this course?
faqs.answer: This section is the foundation for everything ahead. In the next sections, you'll learn function notation (a shorthand for talking about functions) in FN2, how to read information from graphs in FN3, how to transform graphs in FN4, how to combine and compose functions in FN5, and how to find inverses in FN6. Later, you'll study specific families of functions—linear, polynomial, rational, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric—each with their own behavior and applications. By the end of this course, you'll be able to analyze the behavior of each of these families and use it to solve real problems. Every section builds on the ideas you're learning right now.

guided.title: Function or Not? You Decide First
guided.prompt: I'm learning what makes a relation a function: every input has exactly one output. Two inputs can share an output, but one input cannot have two outputs. Give me five everyday relations, one at a time, each written as "input → output" (for example, a student → their student ID number). Don't say whether they are functions. For each one, I'll decide function or not and explain using the words input and output, and you won't confirm until I've explained. Include at least one where two inputs share an output, and at least one that is not a function. After all five, write your own verdict and reason for each, and make one deliberate mistake in them for me to find. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Why the Vertical Line Test Works
guided.prompt: I'm learning the vertical line test. My notes say a graph represents a function when every vertical line crosses it at most once. Before explaining anything, ask me: what do all the points on one vertical line, like x = 2, have in common? Then ask me what it means if that line hits the graph at two points. After I answer, describe one graph at a time in words: a parabola opening up, a parabola opening left, an oval, a horizontal line, five separate points, and two pieces whose x-values overlap. For each, I'll say whether it passes and, if it fails, name a vertical line that proves it. Then describe two new graphs and give your own verdicts, with one deliberate mistake for me to catch. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Extension: Domain with a Square Root and a Fraction
guided.prompt: This goes beyond my FN1 CheckIt exercise. I'm learning to find the domain of a function that has both a square root and a fraction, like f(x) = sqrt(x + 1)/(x - 3). Ask me guiding questions one at a time: what can't go under a square root, what can't go in a denominator, and how to combine the two conditions. Don't give me the answer until I've tried each step. When I have a domain in interval notation, give me f(x) = sqrt(5 - x)/(x + 2) to do on my own. Then write your own solution to one of the two, with one deliberate mistake (such as a wrong bracket or a forgotten restriction) for me to find. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Grade a Classmate's FN1 Answers
guided.prompt: I'm practising the FN1 CheckIt exercise: deciding whether a relation, equation, or graph defines a function, and explaining why. Play a classmate who shows me five answers, one at a time, each with a one-sentence reason: (1) a table of six (x, y) pairs using whole numbers from 1 to 20, (2) a list of six ordered pairs using whole numbers from 1 to 20, (3) a mapping diagram described in words, with six inputs and six outputs, (4) an equation of the form a*y^n + b*x^m = 0, where a and b are whole numbers from 1 to 5 and one of n and m is odd and the other even, each from 2 to 7, and (5) a graph described in words. Make exactly two of the five answers wrong using common mistakes, such as calling it "not a function" because an output repeats, or deciding an equation by the power on x. Don't tell me which ones. For each answer, I'll say right or wrong and fix the reason. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Where Functions Come Back
guided.prompt: I just learned what makes a relation a function and how to use the vertical line test. Show me one specific place this idea comes back later in precalculus or calculus, such as inverse functions or the slope of a graph at a point. Before you explain, ask me to guess why "one output for each input" would matter there, and wait for my guess. Then explain in four or five sentences. I'll check one claim you make against my notes or my course page and tell you what I checked and what I found. If I find something wrong or unclear, correct it and explain the fix.

open.title: Create Your Own
open.prompt: Use the AI tool of your choice. Start by describing what you're confused about or curious about from Section FN1 (Is a Relation a Function?). Ask the AI to question you instead of explaining. Before you trust anything, check one claim the AI makes against your notes or a CheckIt answer (for example, whether a vertical line it names really hits the graph twice, or whether an x-value it tests really gives two y-values), and write down what you checked and what you found.

paths.label: FN1: Introduction to Functions
paths.intro: Builds to the FN1 check: deciding whether mappings, tables, ordered pairs, equations, and graphs define functions, and explaining why. Practice scope: every stop practises the three parts of the FN1 CheckIt exercise: mappings, tables and ordered pairs; equations with one power of y and one power of x; and graphs. Nothing in the path goes beyond it.

stages.desc: Two quick skills FN1 leans on. Skip any you already have.

stops.title: Inputs and outputs in ordered pairs
stops.target: In an ordered pair \((x, y)\), the first number is the input and the second is the output.
stops.cold:
Write the pairs from this table as ordered pairs \((x, y)\).
\(x\)\(2\)\(5\)\(8\)
\(y\)\(4\)\(-1\)\(4\)
stops.coldPlain: Write the pairs from this table as ordered pairs (x, y). x: 2, 5, 8 | y: 4, -1, 4
stops.solution: Each column is one pair, input (x) first and output (y) second: (2, 4), (5, -1), (8, 4).
stops.again: List the inputs and the outputs of \(\{(-1, 6),\ (0, 3),\ (4, 6)\}\).
stops.againA: Inputs: \(-1, 0, 4\). Outputs: \(6, 3\) (the output 6 appears twice, which is allowed).
stops.reflect: How do you know which number in a pair is the input?

stops.title: How many solutions?
stops.target: Know that an even power set equal to a positive number, like \(y^2 = 9\), has two real solutions (\(\pm\)), while an odd power like \(y^3 = 8\) has exactly one.
stops.cold: Solve \(y^2 = 9\) and \(y^3 = 8\). How many solutions does each have?
stops.coldPlain: Solve y^2 = 9 and y^3 = 8. How many solutions does each have?
stops.coldA: \(y^2 = 9\) gives \(y = 3\) or \(y = -3\): two solutions. \(y^3 = 8\) gives only \(y = 2\): cubing keeps the sign and never gives the same value twice, so 2 is the only real cube root of 8.
stops.solution: y^2 = 9: both 3^2 and (-3)^2 equal 9, so y = 3 or y = -3 (two solutions). y^3 = 8: 2^3 = 8 but (-2)^3 = -8, so y = 2 is the only real solution.
stops.mistake: Forgetting the negative solution for an even power, or adding a negative solution for an odd power.
stops.againA: \(y^4 = 16\) gives \(y = \pm 2\) (two solutions). \(y^4 = -16\) has no real solutions, because a fourth power is never negative. \(y^5 = -32\) gives \(y = -2\) (one solution).
stops.reflect: Why can an even power give two solutions when an odd power gives only one? When does an even power give fewer than two?

stages.desc: One stop per type of question on the FN1 check, in order.

stops.title: The definition, with mapping diagrams
stops.target: A relation is a function when every input has exactly one output. Two inputs can share an output; one input cannot have two outputs.
stops.cold: Does this mapping define a function? Explain why.[[graph:M1]]
stops.coldPlain: Does this mapping diagram define a function? Explain why.
stops.graphNote: Mapping diagram with inputs 1, 4, 7, 9 and outputs 2, 5, 8. The arrows go: 1 -> 5, 4 -> 2, 7 -> 5, 9 -> 8.
stops.coldA: Yes. Each input has exactly one arrow. Inputs 1 and 7 both go to 5, and that is allowed.
stops.solution: Check each input: 1 goes only to 5, 4 only to 2, 7 only to 5, 9 only to 8. Every input has exactly one output, so it is a function. Two inputs (1 and 7) sharing the output 5 does not break the rule.
stops.mistake: Thinking that two inputs going to the same output means it is not a function.
stops.again: Does this mapping define a function? Explain why.[[graph:M2]]
stops.againA: No. The input 6 has two outputs, 1 and 15.
stops.reflect: In your own words: what is the one thing that stops a relation from being a function?

stops.title: Tables and ordered pairs
stops.target: Decide whether a table or a list of ordered pairs is a function by looking for a repeated input with different outputs.
stops.cold:
Does this table define \(y\) as a function of \(x\)? Explain why.
\(x\)\(4\)\(11\)\(7\)\(2\)\(11\)\(15\)
\(y\)\(9\)\(3\)\(9\)\(16\)\(8\)\(1\)
stops.coldPlain: Does this table define y as a function of x? Explain why. x: 4, 11, 7, 2, 11, 15 | y: 9, 3, 9, 16, 8, 1
stops.coldA: No. The input \(x = 11\) appears twice, with outputs 3 and 8. (The output 9 appearing twice is fine.)
stops.solution: Scan the inputs for repeats. x = 11 appears twice, paired with y = 3 and y = 8. One input with two outputs means it is not a function. The repeated output 9 (from x = 4 and x = 7) does not matter.
stops.mistake: Scanning the outputs for repeats instead of the inputs.
stops.again: Do these ordered pairs define a function? Explain why. \(\{(5, 12),\ (-3, 7),\ (8, 12),\ (0, -3),\ (7, 5),\ (2, 7)\}\)
stops.againA: Yes. All six inputs (\(5, -3, 8, 0, 7, 2\)) are different. The repeated outputs 12 and 7 are allowed.
stops.stretch: Change one pair in that list so it is not a function.
stops.stretchA: Answers vary. Reuse an input with a new output, for example change \((2, 7)\) to \((5, 1)\), so the input 5 has outputs 12 and 1.
stops.reflect: Which list do you scan for repeats, the inputs or the outputs? Why?

stops.title: Equations: solve for y
stops.target: Decide whether an equation defines \(y\) as a function of \(x\) by solving for \(y\). If solving for \(y\) needs an even root, some inputs give two outputs (\(\pm\)), so it is not a function. If it needs an odd root, every input gives exactly one output.
stops.cold:
Does each equation define \(y\) as a function of \(x\)? Explain why.
(a) \(2y^3 = 16x^2\)    (b) \(2x^3 = 16y^2\)
stops.coldPlain: Does each equation define y as a function of x? Explain why. (a) 2y^3 = 16x^2   (b) 2x^3 = 16y^2
stops.coldA: (a) Yes. \(y^3 = 8x^2\), so \(y = \sqrt[3]{8x^2}\): one output for each input. (b) No. \(y^2 = \frac{x^3}{8}\), so \(y = \pm\sqrt{\frac{x^3}{8}}\) for \(x \ge 0\) (negative \(x\) gives no \(y\)). For example, \(x = 2\) gives \(y = 1\) and \(y = -1\).
stops.solution: (a) Solve for y: y^3 = 8x^2, so y = cube root of (8x^2). A cube root gives exactly one value, so each x gives one y: a function. Check: x = 1 gives y^3 = 8, so y = 2 only. (b) Solve for y: y^2 = x^3/8, so y = +/- sqrt(x^3/8) (for x >= 0). Check: x = 2 gives 16 = 16y^2, so y^2 = 1 and y = 1 or y = -1. One input, two outputs: not a function.
stops.mistake: Deciding based on the power of x instead of the power of y, or forgetting the +/- when taking an even root.
stops.again:
Does each equation define \(y\) as a function of \(x\)?
(a) \(4y^4 + x^3 = 0\)    (b) \(y^5 - 2x^4 = 0\)
stops.againA: (a) No. \(y^4 = -\frac{x^3}{4}\). Positive \(x\) gives no \(y\) at all, so try a negative one: \(x = -4\) gives \(y^4 = 16\), so \(y = 2\) or \(y = -2\). (b) Yes. \(y^5 = 2x^4\), so \(y = \sqrt[5]{2x^4}\): one output for each input.
stops.reflect: Where do you look in an equation to decide quickly, and what are you looking for?

stops.title: The vertical line test
stops.target: A graph is a function when every vertical line crosses it at most once. If some vertical line crosses twice, one input has two outputs. CheckIt draws its graphs without arrowheads or endpoint dots: a curve that reaches the edge of the window keeps going, and a piece that stops inside the window stops there.
stops.cold: Which of these graphs represent functions? Explain each one.[[graph:ROW1]]
stops.coldPlain: Which of these three graphs represent functions? Explain each one.
stops.graphNote: Graph (a): An upward-opening parabola with vertex (1, -4), crossing the x-axis at (-1, 0) and (3, 0); both branches continue upward. Graph (b): A parabola opening to the left, x = 2 - y^2, with vertex (2, 0), passing through (-2, 2) and (-2, -2). Graph (c): Five separate points: (-4, -2), (-1, 3), (2, 1), (5, 4), (5, -2).
stops.coldA: (a) Yes: every vertical line crosses it exactly once. (b) No: the line \(x = -2\) crosses at \((-2, 2)\) and \((-2, -2)\). (c) No: the points \((5, 4)\) and \((5, -2)\) share the input 5.
stops.solution: (a) Upward parabola: every vertical line hits it exactly once, so it is a function. (b) Parabola opening to the left: the vertical line x = -2 hits (-2, 2) and (-2, -2), so it is not a function. (c) Points: the vertical line x = 5, at the right edge of the grid, hits (5, 4) and (5, -2), so it is not a function.
stops.mistake: Using a horizontal line instead of a vertical line, or forgetting that the test applies to separate points too.
stops.again: Which of these graphs represent functions? Explain each one.[[graph:ROW2]]
stops.againA: (a) Yes: the cubic passes the vertical line test. (b) No: vertical lines strictly between \(x = -2\) and \(x = 4\) cross the oval twice; for example \(x = 1\) crosses at \((1, 1)\) and \((1, -3)\). (c) No: the two pieces overlap between \(x = 0\) and \(x = 1\), so a vertical line there (like \(x = 0.5\), at \((0.5, -1.875)\) and \((0.5, 1.5)\)) crosses both.
stops.stretchA: Yes. All five points have different \(x\)-values, so no vertical line hits two of them.
stops.reflect: Why does a vertical line test for "one output per input"?

stages.desc: A practice check in the same three-part format as the FN1 CheckIt exercise.

stops.title: Practice check
stops.target: Decide whether relations, equations, and graphs are functions, and explain why, the way the FN1 check asks. On CheckIt, answer in a full sentence with a reason, for example: "This table does not define a function, because the input 7 has two outputs, 2 and 11."
stops.cold:
Part 1. Explain why each relation does or does not define a function.
(a)[[graph:M3]](b)
\(x\)\(3\)\(8\)\(12\)\(1\)\(17\)\(6\)
\(y\)\(5\)\(5\)\(14\)\(9\)\(2\)\(14\)
(c) \(\{(4, 10),\ (9, 2),\ (15, 10),\ (4, 7),\ (20, 1),\ (11, 13)\}\)

Part 2. Explain why each equation does or does not define \(y\) as a function of \(x\): (a) \(4y^7 + 3x^2 = 0\)   (b) \(x^3 + 4y^2 = 0\)

Part 3. Explain why each graph does or does not represent a function.[[graph:ROW3]]
stops.coldPlain: Part 1: Explain why each relation does or does not define a function: (a) a mapping diagram, (b) a table: x: 3, 8, 12, 1, 17, 6 | y: 5, 5, 14, 9, 2, 14, (c) {(4, 10), (9, 2), (15, 10), (4, 7), (20, 1), (11, 13)}. Part 2: Does each equation define y as a function of x? (a) 4y^7 + 3x^2 = 0, (b) x^3 + 4y^2 = 0. Part 3: Does each of three graphs represent a function?
stops.graphNote: Part 1(a): Mapping diagram with inputs 3, 7, 12, 16 and outputs 4, 9, 14, 17, 19. The arrows go: 3 -> 9, 7 -> 4, 12 -> 19, 16 -> 9, 16 -> 14. No arrow goes to 17. Part 3: Graph (a): A horizontal line y = -3. Graph (b): A hyperbola y^2 - x^2 = 1 with two branches, one opening up from (0, 1) and one opening down from (0, -1). Graph (c): Two pieces: the parabola y = x^2 - 3 coming down from the top edge to a solid dot at (0, -3), and the line y = -x + 4 from a solid dot at (1, 3) to the right edge.

1. (a) No: input 16 has two outputs, 9 and 14. (The output 17 with no arrow, and 3 and 16 sharing the output 9, are both fine.) (b) Yes: all inputs are different. (c) No: input 4 has outputs 10 and 7.

stops.solution: Part 1: (a) Not a function: input 16 maps to both 9 and 14. An output with no arrow (17) and two inputs sharing an output (3 and 16 both go to 9) are allowed. (b) Function: inputs 3, 8, 12, 1, 17, 6 are all different (repeated outputs 5 and 14 are fine). (c) Not a function: input 4 appears with outputs 10 and 7. Part 2: (a) 4y^7 + 3x^2 = 0 gives y^7 = -3x^2/4, so y = seventh root of (-3x^2/4). An odd root gives exactly one value, so each x has one output: a function. (b) x^3 + 4y^2 = 0 gives y^2 = -x^3/4. Positive x gives no y at all, so test a negative x: x = -4 gives y^2 = 16, so y = 4 or y = -4. One input, two outputs: not a function. Part 3: (a) the horizontal line y = -3 is a function: every x gives y = -3. (b) the hyperbola fails: x = 0 hits (0, 1) and (0, -1). (c) the two pieces have a gap between x = 0 and x = 1 and do not overlap, so every vertical line crosses at most once: a function.
stops.mistake: Saying "not a function" because an output repeats or an output has no arrow, deciding an equation by the power on x, testing only positive x in an equation like x^3 + 4y^2 = 0 (where positive x gives no y at all), or checking each piece of a piecewise graph separately instead of the whole graph at once.
